CASE 03 · FRACTURE CARE

Elbow fracture: radial head fixation with a compression screw

A split fracture of the radial head in the left elbow, repaired with a single buried compression screw so the elbow could start moving early.

  • Area: Left elbow
  • Procedure: Screw fixation (ORIF)
  • Bone healing: 6–8 weeks
Read the case ↓

The radial head is the disc-shaped top of the radius, the forearm bone on the thumb side. It turns against the end of the upper-arm bone each time you rotate your palm up or down. A fall on an outstretched hand is the most common cause of a break here.

Condition
Radial head fracture (partial joint-surface split)
Treatment
Fixation with a headless compression screw
Movement starts
Within the first few days
Hospital stay
Usually 1–2 days
Bone healing
About 6–8 weeks
Final result
3–6 months

Tap or click an image to view it full size.

01

What the X-rays at diagnosis show

The top two images are the front view and side view of the left elbow (marked “L”, with a 9 cm measuring scale):

  • A split through the radial head: a fracture line runs down through the radial head, separating part of the joint surface from the rest of the bone.
  • A step in the joint surface: the broken piece no longer lines up with the rest of the head. Even a small step here can catch during forearm rotation and wear the joint early.
  • Rest of the elbow: the upper-arm bone (humerus) and the ulna appear intact, and the elbow joint is in position. This matters because it means the injury can be repaired directly.
02

Why surgery was chosen

Small, undisplaced radial head cracks usually heal in a sling with early movement. When a fragment of the joint surface has shifted, as here, fixing it gives the best chance of smooth, pain-free rotation and prevents a mechanical block or early arthritis.

03

The procedure

Through a small incision on the outer side of the elbow, the fragment is lifted back into its exact position, restoring a smooth joint surface. It is then held with a headless compression screw. This screw has threads at both ends, so it pulls the fragments tightly together, and it sits fully buried below the cartilage so it does not rub on the joint.

04

What the images during surgery confirm

The bottom two images were taken in the operating theatre with a live X-ray (fluoroscopy):

  • Front view (bottom left): the screw crosses the fracture line at a right angle, which gives the strongest compression across the break.
  • Side view (bottom right): the screw lies fully within the radial head, with its ends inside the bone and nothing protruding into the joint.
  • Restored surface: the fragment is back in line, so the radial head can rotate smoothly again.

Recovery and healing timeline

Every recovery is individual. These are the typical stages, and your own plan will be adjusted at each follow-up visit.

Wound healingAbout 10–14 daysStitches removed at the first review
Bone healingAbout 6–8 weeksConfirmed on follow-up X-ray
Full recoveryAbout 3–4 monthsFinal movement by 3–6 months
  1. Days 0–3

    Sling for comfort, fingers moving

    A sling supports the arm for comfort only. Finger, wrist and shoulder exercises start immediately to reduce swelling and stiffness.

  2. Days 3–7

    Gentle elbow movement

    Because the fixation is stable, gentle bending, straightening and forearm rotation usually begin within the first week. The elbow stiffens easily, so early movement is the key to a good result.

  3. Weeks 2

    Wound review

    Stitches are removed at about 10–14 days. The sling is usually no longer needed. Light daily tasks such as eating and writing are encouraged.

  4. Weeks 2–6

    Regaining range of motion

    Regular physiotherapy to recover full bending, straightening and palm-up/palm-down rotation. Avoid lifting more than about 1 kg or pushing up from a chair with the arm.

  5. Weeks 6–8

    Bone healing confirmed

    A follow-up X-ray usually shows the fracture has united. Strengthening exercises are then added gradually.

  6. Weeks 8–12

    Return to work and lifting

    Progressive return to lifting, most work and driving. Manual workers may need a little longer.

  7. Months 3–6

    Final result

    Range of motion and grip strength continue to improve. Most people regain functional movement; the last few degrees of straightening can take several months.

05

Helping your recovery at home

  • Move the fingers, wrist and shoulder many times a day from day one.
  • Follow the physiotherapy plan closely; elbow stiffness is the most common problem after this injury.
  • Do not force or massage the elbow aggressively, and avoid heavy lifting until bone healing is confirmed.
  • The buried screw normally stays in place permanently and does not need removal.

When to contact the clinic urgently

  • Fever, or increasing redness, warmth or discharge from the wound
  • Calf pain or swelling, or sudden chest pain or breathlessness (seek emergency care)
  • New numbness, tingling, or a cold or pale limb
  • A sudden increase in pain, a new deformity, or being unable to move or bear weight as before
